one_liner: CUDA sparse LU numeric factorization for circuit matrices; papers report 19.56x over KLU (numeric phase only, float32).
what_it_does: GLU3.0 factorizes a square sparse matrix in four stages: NICSLU preprocessing on the CPU (MC64-style static row permutation and scaling, AMD ordering), CPU symbolic fill-in and levelization, GPU numeric factorization, then CPU forward/back substitution. It ships as a command-line program (lu_cmd -i matrix.mtx [-p], right-hand side fixed to all ones, answer written to x.dat) and as pyglu Python bindings with a scipy-like splu(A).solve(b) and spsolve(A, b, perturb=...). There is no installable C/C++ library API; C++ users call the internal Symbolic_Matrix and LUonDevice functions directly, and nothing mirrors KLU's analyze/factor/refactor/solve split.
how_it_is_fast: A hybrid right-looking column algorithm: symbolic analysis predicts the L+U pattern and groups columns into dependency-free levels (with GLU2.0's double-U dependency check, relaxed in 3.0), so all columns of a level are factorized at once and their submatrix updates are applied with atomicAdd. GLU3.0 adapts the kernel shape to each level: more than 896 columns use 2 warps per block, more than 448 use 4, more than 16 use 32, and the last 16 or fewer columns run as single-column kernels across 16 CUDA streams with 1024 threads each. Values are float32 because the Maxwell GPU used for the paper had no FP64 atomics; the paper expects FP64 to be about 30 percent slower. The TVLSI paper notes part of its large speedups (up to 530x over KLU on mc2depi) comes from denormal numbers that slow the CPU solvers down.
when_to_use: Large, low-fill circuit-simulation matrices (tens of thousands to millions of rows) on an NVIDIA GPU where numeric factorization dominates: the GLU3.0 paper measured 2.9x to 10.5x over 32-thread NICSLU on ASIC_320ks, ASIC_680ks and G3_circuit.
Research or prototyping of GPU LU where you will edit the C++/CUDA to reuse one symbolic analysis across many Newton-iteration refactorizations, since the shipped CLI and pyglu redo it every call.
Python code that wants a GPU splu/spsolve with a SciPy-like call and can live with float32 accuracy.
Matrices whose CPU factorization is slowed by denormal values (barrier2-11 in the TVLSI paper).
When you need modifiable source under a permissive license: the GLU code is BSD-3-Clause (the bundled NICSLU is LGPL-2.1).
when_not_to_use: When you need double precision: REAL is typedef float, inputs are cast to float32, the CPU triangular solves run in float32 with no iterative refinement, and issue #2 reported a log-determinant differing from MATLAB at about 1e-9 relative on the 4,960-row add32 example.

One-shot solves: CPU preprocessing and symbolic time dwarfs the GPU numeric time (9,729 ms vs 878 ms on G3_circuit, 7,241 ms vs 845 ms on Raj1 in the GLU3.0 paper's Table I), and pyglu repeats it on every splu call.

Small circuits such as circuit_2 and rajat15, where the TVLSI paper says GLU is slower than the CPU solvers; on Raj1 and rajat20 the GLU3.0 numeric time only ties 32-thread NICSLU (0.98x, 1.02x), and on general matrices GLU 1.0 was only 1.12x over 16-thread PARDISO.

Matrices that need dynamic partial pivoting: the GPU phase does no pivoting and relies on the static MC64-style permutation, plus optional perturbation of tiny pivots to 3.45e-4 times the 1-norm of A (-p / perturb=True).

Matrices whose nnz approaches 2^32 or whose L+U factors exceed GPU memory (32-bit unsigned indices, issue #3 open), complex-valued systems (issue #5 open), and non-NVIDIA GPUs or non-x86 hosts (NICSLU is built with -msse2).

integration.form: source-drop: src/Makefile builds the lu_cmd executable against bundled NICSLU static libraries; setup.py builds the pyglu Python extension
integration.dependencies: CUDA toolkit (nvcc, cudart), bundled NICSLU (LGPL-2.1), pthread, libm, librt; pyglu adds Python >= 3.9, pybind11 >= 2.11, NumPy >= 1.22 and optional SciPy >= 1.9
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (g++ -std=c++11 -O3, nvcc -O3 -std=c++11); minimum CUDA version not documented (the TVLSI work used CUDA 5.0)
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 with one NVIDIA GPU; the build passes no -arch flag, so nvcc's default target applies; LUonDevice always uses device 0
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; each LUonDevice call allocates and frees its own device buffers on device 0, and memory sizing assumes it is the only user of the GPU
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — pyglu mirrors scipy.sparse.linalg.splu/spsolve (float64 in and out, float32 inside), but there is no KLU- or UMFPACK-style C API with separate analyze, factor, refactor and solve calls

gotchas: LUonDevice sizes its dense scratch buffer (tmpMem, one n-length float column per in-flight column) to fit all free GPU memory except 4 GB, or half the free memory when less than 4 GB is free, so a second process or factorization on the same GPU can fail (inferred from numeric.cu).

Numerical failures can pass silently: pyglu scans the factors for NaN/Inf only when a CUDA error message was produced, and the NaN check in numeric.cu sits behind GLU_DEBUG, which the Makefile passes only to g++, not to nvcc (inferred from the source). Submatrix updates use float atomicAdd, so results are not bit-reproducible run to run.
Issue #6 (open since May 2023): a matrix written row-wise (CSR) to .mtx gave wrong solutions, while the same matrix in CSC matched SciPy; feed CSC data.

The February 2026 fixes (a __syncthreads() on a divergent path that could deadlock, unchecked CUDA calls, unsafe scratch sizing) mean pre-2026 checkouts, which the papers measured, can hang or mis-size memory; use current master.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: NICSLU (1.87x over KLU, CPU) is the stronger choice for one-off solves: the GLU3.0 paper puts GLU's numeric phase at 2.81x geometric mean over 32-thread NICSLU, but GLU's CPU preprocessing and symbolic time alone often exceeds NICSLU's whole numeric factorization (7,241 ms vs 825 ms on Raj1). CKTSO-GPU claims 13.29x geometric mean refactorization over KLU 1.3.9 on the same circuit workload. Pick GLU when you want BSD-3-Clause GPU source to modify or a SciPy-style Python entry point, and float32 accuracy is acceptable.
verified_claims_summary: TVLSI 2016 (GLU 1.0, PDF in docs/): numeric factorization time only, excluding preprocessing and symbolic analysis, on a Tesla K40 (CUDA 5.0) against CPU solvers on two 8-core Xeon E5-2670: 19.56x over KLU 1.2.0 and 47.13x over UMFPACK 5.6.2 on typical UFL circuit matrices, 39.39x and 24.04x on general matrices. GLU3.0 (IEEE D&T 2020, GTX TITAN X, -O3, float32): numeric factorization including memory copies averages 2.81x geometric mean (3.51x arithmetic) faster than 32-thread NICSLU on 15 circuit matrices, with the larger CPU preprocessing and symbolic times reported separately; neither paper measured the current repo code.
status_note: UC Riverside research code that sat dormant from 2020 to 2026, then got Codex-assisted bug fixes (Feb 2026), pyglu bindings (Mar 2026) and a GitHub Pages site (Jul 2026); 12 commits, no CI tests (the only workflow publishes Pages), 5 open issues, BSD-3-Clause GLU code bundling LGPL-2.1 NICSLU.
